questions.stem: Which leaders, often called the Big Three, dominated decision-making at the Paris Peace Conference of 1919?
options: Wilson, Lloyd George and Mussolini
Roosevelt, Churchill and Clemenceau too
Lenin, Lloyd George and Clemenceau
Wilson, Lloyd George and Clemenceau
questions.explanation: President Wilson of the USA, Prime Minister Lloyd George of Britain and Premier Clemenceau of France shaped the main decisions, with Orlando of Italy playing a smaller part. Roosevelt and Churchill belong to the Second World War, and Soviet Russia was not invited.

questions.stem: Germans called the Treaty of Versailles a 'diktat' mainly because:
options: it was drafted in secret by the German Kaiser's own ministers
it was voted down by the German National Assembly
it was imposed only after Germany had invaded France
Germany was not allowed to negotiate its terms
questions.explanation: The German delegation was handed the terms and had to sign under threat of renewed war, so Germans saw it as a dictated peace. The National Assembly reluctantly accepted it, and the Kaiser had already abdicated in November 1918.

questions.stem: Which set of terms was imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles?
options: an army of 100,000, no air force, and a demilitarised Rhineland
an army of 300,000, a small air force, and an occupied Bavaria
full disarmament, a ban on all police, and an occupied Prussia
an army of 100,000, no navy at all, and the loss of East Prussia
questions.explanation: The treaty limited the army to 100,000 men, banned an air force, tanks and submarines, and demilitarised the Rhineland. Germany kept a small navy and kept East Prussia, which was cut off from the rest of Germany by the Polish Corridor.

questions.stem: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles was especially resented in Germany because it:
options: set up the League of Nations without allowing Germany to join it
forbade the union of Germany and Austria under any circumstances
assigned responsibility for the war's loss and damage to Germany and its allies
handed the province of Alsace-Lorraine back to France without any vote by its people
questions.explanation: Article 231, the 'war guilt' clause, held Germany and its allies responsible for the loss and damage of the war and was the legal basis for reparations. The other terms were real grievances too, but the guilt clause was felt as a national humiliation.

questions.stem: Why did many Italians call the outcome of the Paris Peace Conference a 'mutilated victory'?
options: Italy gained less territory than it had expected, including Fiume and most of Dalmatia
Italy was forced to pay heavy reparations to Austria for the damage done along the Isonzo front
Italy lost South Tyrol to the new state of Austria under the Treaty of Saint-Germain
Italy was excluded from the conference and the treaty was signed without it
questions.explanation: Italy had joined the Allies in 1915 on promises of territory, and nationalists were angry that it did not receive Fiume or most of Dalmatia. Italy in fact gained South Tyrol and Trieste, and Orlando attended the conference, but resentment of the settlement fed the Fascist movement.

questions.stem: In 1919 the economist John Maynard Keynes condemned the reparations imposed on Germany. Historians such as Margaret MacMillan have since argued that:
options: the treaty did not make the Second World War inevitable; later choices mattered more
the treaty was far too lenient and should have broken Germany into smaller states
the reparations were never demanded, so the treaty had no economic effect at all
the treaty was the single direct cause of the Second World War that broke out twenty years later
questions.explanation: Keynes argued that the reparations would ruin Germany and harm all of Europe. MacMillan and other historians argue that the settlement was a compromise and that the decisions of leaders in the 1930s, above all Hitler, did more to cause the war. Reparations were in fact demanded and partly paid.

questions.stem: Which consequence of the peace settlements best shows how they could help dictators gain support?
options: The League of Nations used its own standing army to enforce the treaties against every aggressor state
The USA joined the League of Nations and guaranteed the new borders of eastern Europe
Every new state in eastern Europe was made ethnically uniform by the new borders
Nationalists in Germany and Italy used resentment of the treaties to attack democratic governments
questions.explanation: Resentment of the 'diktat' in Germany and the 'mutilated victory' in Italy let nationalist movements portray democratic leaders as weak or traitorous. The League had no army, the US Senate kept the USA out of it, and the new states contained large minorities.

questions.stem: Which development after 1917 made many middle-class and propertied Europeans willing to support authoritarian movements?
options: fear of a return to absolute monarchy across Europe
fear that women would lose the vote they had only just won
fear that the League of Nations would abolish armies
fear of a communist revolution like the one in Russia
questions.explanation: The Bolshevik seizure of power and the wave of strikes and uprisings that followed made property owners, industrialists and the Church fear revolution. Movements that promised to crush the left, such as Mussolini's Fascists, gained their backing.

questions.stem: Which feature of several new interwar democracies, including Weimar Germany, tended to produce weak and short-lived governments?
options: compulsory voting forcing extremists to join the major parties
hereditary upper houses with the power to veto every new law
proportional representation creating many parties and unstable coalitions
first-past-the-post voting giving one single party a permanent and large majority
questions.explanation: Pure proportional representation let many small parties win seats, so governments relied on fragile coalitions that often collapsed. Voters who saw parliaments as chaotic were more open to leaders promising strong rule.

questions.stem: Returned soldiers were important to the rise of interwar dictators mainly because many of them:
options: were given reserved seats in parliament as a reward for their war service
were sent to the colonies and so were absent from European politics
joined paramilitary groups that used violence against political opponents
refused to take part in politics and stayed out of all public life
questions.explanation: Unemployed and embittered veterans filled groups such as Italy's Blackshirt squads and Germany's Freikorps and later the SA. Their organised violence intimidated opponents and made extremist movements seem a force for order against the left.

questions.stem: A historian argues that dictators came to power in the interwar period mainly because traditional elites invited them in. Which evidence best supports this argument?
options: Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini, and Hindenburg appointed Hitler, on elite advice
Mussolini and Hitler each won a clear majority of the votes cast in a free national election
Mussolini and Hitler each seized power through a successful armed revolution
The armies of Italy and Germany fought Fascist and Nazi squads to defend the parliament
questions.explanation: Both men were appointed legally by heads of state who hoped to use them against the left. Neither won a majority in a free election; the March on Rome was a threat rather than a battle, and Hitler's 1923 putsch had failed.

questions.stem: During the 'Biennio Rosso' (two red years) of 1919-1920 in Italy:
options: the Catholic Church and the Italian state signed the Lateran Pacts
workers occupied factories and peasants seized land amid waves of strikes
Mussolini's Fascists won a majority of seats in the Chamber of Deputies
Italy fought a short war against the new Yugoslavia over the port of Trieste
questions.explanation: Strikes, factory occupations in the north and land seizures frightened industrialists and landowners, who began funding Fascist squads to break the left. The Lateran Pacts came much later, in 1929.

questions.stem: The Fascist 'March on Rome' of October 1922 led to Mussolini becoming Prime Minister because:
options: Mussolini won an absolute majority of seats in that month's election
the Pope publicly called on all Italian Catholics to support the Fascist takeover of power
King Victor Emmanuel III refused to declare martial law and invited him to govern
the Fascists defeated the Italian army in street battles in the capital
questions.explanation: The army could probably have stopped the poorly armed marchers, but the king refused to sign the martial law decree and appointed Mussolini instead. The Fascists then held only a small number of seats in parliament.

questions.stem: The Acerbo Law of 1923 strengthened Mussolini's position by:
options: allowing Mussolini to rule by personal decree without consulting the Chamber for four full years
giving the vote to all Italian women, who were expected to support the Fascists
giving two-thirds of the seats to the party list that won the most votes, if at least 25%
banning every party except the National Fascist Party from contesting elections
questions.explanation: The law gave a list with the largest share, provided it reached 25%, two-thirds of the seats. In the 1924 election the government list easily won its majority. Other parties were banned only in 1926.

questions.stem: How did the murder of the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti in 1924 become a turning point for Fascist Italy?
options: It caused the king to dismiss Mussolini and appoint a socialist government
It led Mussolini to restore press freedom and allow genuinely free elections again
It brought Italy into an alliance with Germany against the Western powers
After the crisis Mussolini took responsibility and moved to a full dictatorship
questions.explanation: Opposition deputies walked out in the Aventine Secession, but the king did nothing. In January 1925 Mussolini accepted responsibility for what had happened, and over 1925-26 laws banned other parties, censored the press and created a police state.

questions.stem: The Lateran Pacts of 1929 between Mussolini and the Papacy:
options: made the Pope a joint head of state of Italy alongside King Victor Emmanuel III
forced all Catholic priests to join the National Fascist Party
recognised Vatican City as independent and made Catholicism the state religion
abolished the Catholic Church's role in Italian schools and in marriage
questions.explanation: The agreements ended the dispute between Church and state dating from 1870, created the independent Vatican City and confirmed Catholicism as the state religion. They won Mussolini the goodwill of many Catholics.

questions.stem: Historians often describe Fascist Italy as an 'imperfect' totalitarian state. Which feature best supports this view?
options: The monarchy, the Church and the army kept independent sources of power
Mussolini held elections in which opposition parties regularly won seats
Fascist Italy had no secret police and no censorship of the press
Mussolini refused to build a personality cult around himself as Duce
questions.explanation: Mussolini never controlled the king, who dismissed him in 1943, and the Lateran Pacts left the Church with its own organisations and loyalty. Italy did have secret police, censorship and a cult of the Duce, so those cannot support the view.

questions.stem: Which policy was part of Mussolini's corporate state and economic program?
options: the free movement of foreign goods into Italy without tariffs
the 'Battle for Grain' to make Italy self-sufficient in wheat
the collectivisation of all peasant farms into state cooperatives
the abolition of private ownership of factories and banks
questions.explanation: The Battle for Grain, launched in 1925, raised wheat output as part of a drive for self-sufficiency. Fascism kept private property and organised employers and workers into state-controlled corporations; collectivisation was a Soviet policy.

questions.stem: Which position, held from 1922, gave Stalin the power to appoint party officials and build support before Lenin's death?
options: Commissar for War and the Red Army
Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars
Head of the Cheka secret police
General Secretary of the Communist Party
questions.explanation: As General Secretary Stalin controlled appointments and promotions, filling the party with loyal officials who voted for him. Trotsky was Commissar for War, and Lenin chaired the Council of People's Commissars.

questions.stem: In the power struggle after Lenin's death in 1924, Stalin's policy of 'Socialism in One Country' meant:
options: building socialism within the USSR first rather than spreading world revolution
returning all industry to private ownership to rebuild the Soviet economy
allowing each Soviet republic to choose its own separate form of socialism by a free vote
joining with Western socialist parties in a single international government
questions.explanation: Stalin argued the USSR should build socialism on its own, an appealing message after years of war. It contrasted with Trotsky's 'permanent revolution', which stressed spreading revolution abroad.

questions.stem: In the years after 1928, Stalin's collectivisation of agriculture involved:
options: paying peasants high market prices to encourage them to grow grain
forcing peasants into collective farms and deporting those labelled kulaks
giving each peasant family its own private plot of land to farm and sell for profit
returning the great estates to the former noble landowners
questions.explanation: Peasants were forced onto collective farms, and millions branded kulaks were deported or killed. Resistance, falling output and grain requisitioning led to famine in 1932-33, most severely in Ukraine and Kazakhstan.

questions.stem: Which feature did Stalin's Soviet Union and Mussolini's Italy have in common?
options: a single ruling party, propaganda and a cult of the leader
state ownership of all land, factories and banks
a monarch who could legally dismiss the head of government
an alliance with the Catholic Church through a formal treaty
questions.explanation: Both regimes had one party, secret police, censorship, propaganda and a leader cult. Only the USSR abolished private ownership of the economy, and only Italy kept a king and signed a treaty with the Papacy.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the main difference between the ideologies of Fascist Italy and the Soviet Union?
options: Fascism rejected the use of violence; Soviet communism relied on terror and a secret police
Fascism supported parliamentary democracy; Soviet communism supported rule by the king and nobility
Fascism stressed the nation and kept private property; Soviet communism stressed class and abolished it
Fascism promoted international revolution; Soviet communism stressed loyalty to the Russian nation alone
questions.explanation: Fascism glorified the nation and the state while protecting private property and the elites, whereas Soviet communism was based on class struggle and state ownership. Both used violence and terror, so that cannot be the difference.

questions.stem: Between 1936 and 1938 a series of public show trials took place in Moscow. As a source, a published transcript of one of these trials is most useful to a historian as evidence of:
options: the exact number of people executed during the Great Terror
how the regime wanted the public to see its enemies and justify the purges
the true crimes the defendants had committed against the Soviet state
the private opinions held by ordinary Soviet citizens about the leadership of Stalin
questions.explanation: The confessions were produced under pressure and the charges were fabricated, so the transcripts are unreliable about guilt. They are valuable as propaganda that shows how the regime presented its 'enemies'. They give no figures for the wider terror.

questions.stem: The Weimar Republic took its name from the town of Weimar because:
options: it became the permanent capital of Germany in place of Berlin
the National Assembly met there in 1919 to write the new constitution
the Kaiser abdicated there in November 1918 before fleeing to the Netherlands
the armistice ending the First World War was signed there
questions.explanation: Unrest in Berlin led the elected National Assembly to meet in Weimar, where it drafted the constitution adopted in August 1919. Berlin remained the capital, and the armistice was signed in a railway carriage near Compiègne.

questions.stem: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed:
options: the Chancellor to suspend the President's office for the length of a national crisis
the states to leave the Reich if a majority of their voters agreed
the army to choose the Chancellor if the Reichstag could not agree
the President to rule by emergency decree when public order was threatened
questions.explanation: Article 48 gave the President emergency powers to issue decrees and restore order. Used heavily from 1930, it let governments rule without the Reichstag and prepared the way for dictatorship.

questions.stem: The Spartacist Uprising of January 1919 was:
options: a communist revolt in Berlin crushed by the government using the Freikorps
a right-wing attempt to restore the Kaiser that was defeated by a general strike
a Nazi attempt to seize power in Munich that ended in a shoot-out with police
a French-led occupation of the Ruhr to force Germany to pay reparations
questions.explanation: The Spartacists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, rose in Berlin, and the SPD government used the right-wing Freikorps against them; both leaders were killed. The general strike defeated the Kapp Putsch of 1920, and the Munich Putsch was in 1923.

questions.stem: How was the Kapp Putsch of March 1920 defeated?
options: The Reichstag voted to arrest Kapp and the leaders of the Freikorps
A general strike by workers paralysed Berlin and the putschists gave up
The army attacked the putschists and defeated them in fighting in Berlin
French troops entered Berlin and restored the elected government
questions.explanation: The army refused to defend the government, which fled Berlin, but a general strike stopped the city working and the putsch collapsed within days. The episode showed that the army could not be relied on to defend the Republic.

questions.stem: In 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr. Which sequence correctly links the occupation to hyperinflation?
options: Hyperinflation began; Germany missed its payments; occupation; the strikes were ended by the Dawes Plan
Germany refused to disarm; occupation; the Rentenmark was introduced; workers went on strike
Germany left the League of Nations; occupation; the Young Plan collapsed; prices soared
Germany missed reparation deliveries; occupation; passive resistance paid for by printing money
questions.explanation: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr after Germany fell behind on reparations. The government backed passive resistance and paid striking workers by printing money, turning existing inflation into hyperinflation. Germany only joined the League in 1926.

questions.stem: In November 1923 Hitler's Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch:
options: failed, and Hitler was tried and sentenced to five years' imprisonment
succeeded in taking control of Bavaria for several weeks before collapsing
led directly to Hitler's appointment as Chancellor by President Ebert
was supported by the Reichswehr and only ended when the French intervened
questions.explanation: Police stopped the march in Munich, and Hitler was convicted of treason. He served about nine months, wrote Mein Kampf and decided to win power by elections rather than force. The trial also gave him national publicity.

questions.stem: Which policy helped bring about Weimar's 'Golden Years' of 1924-1929?
options: the Four-Year Plan, which prepared the economy for rearmament
the Locarno Pact, which ended the treaty limits on the size of the German army
the Dawes Plan, which rescheduled reparations and brought American loans
the Young Plan, which cancelled reparations and returned the colonies
questions.explanation: The 1924 Dawes Plan eased reparation payments and opened the way to large US loans, which, with the new currency, stabilised the economy. Locarno improved relations with France but did not lift the military limits, and the Four-Year Plan was a Nazi policy.

questions.stem: A historian describes Weimar's recovery after 1924 as 'dancing on a volcano'. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: The Nazis won only a small share of the vote in the Reichstag election of 1928
The economy relied heavily on short-term American loans that could be withdrawn
Germany was admitted to the League of Nations in 1926 as a permanent Council member
Stresemann won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work on the Locarno Treaties
questions.explanation: Dependence on short-term US loans left the economy exposed, and they were recalled after the Wall Street Crash of 1929. League membership, Locarno and the Nazis' weak 1928 result are signs of real stability, so they do not support the metaphor.

questions.stem: In March 1930 Hermann Müller's Grand Coalition government collapsed. Its fall was significant because:
options: it led immediately to Hitler's appointment as Chancellor by Hindenburg
it caused the Allies to reoccupy the Rhineland and to cancel the newly agreed Young Plan
it was the last government before the Kaiser returned from exile
later chancellors governed by presidential decree rather than through the Reichstag
questions.explanation: The coalition split over unemployment insurance as the Depression deepened. Brüning, who followed, governed through Article 48 decrees, which began the shift from parliamentary rule to presidential government.

questions.stem: In the Reichstag election of July 1932 the Nazi Party:
options: was banned from standing by a decree of Hindenburg
became the largest party with about 37% of the vote
won an absolute majority with about 52% of the total vote
came third, behind the SPD and the Communists
questions.explanation: The Nazis won 230 seats and about 37% of the vote, their best result in a fully free election, but not a majority. Their vote fell to about 33% in November 1932.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933?
options: The Reichstag passed an Enabling Act that made Hitler Chancellor and President
The army staged a coup and handed power to Hitler after Schleicher resigned
Papen and other conservatives persuaded Hindenburg, believing they could control Hitler
Hitler defeated Hindenburg in the presidential election of 1932 and then took both of the offices
questions.explanation: After Papen and Schleicher failed to build stable governments, Papen and his allies convinced Hindenburg to appoint Hitler with a cabinet of mostly conservatives. Hindenburg had beaten Hitler in 1932, and the Enabling Act came after the appointment.

questions.stem: Historian A stresses the Weimar Constitution's flaws, such as Article 48. Historian B stresses the Great Depression. Historian C stresses intrigue by a small group of elites around Hindenburg. These historians mainly disagree about:
options: whether Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933
whether the Nazis won many votes in the Reichstag elections of 1930 to 1932
which factor did most to bring about the collapse of the Republic
whether the Weimar Republic collapsed at all before 1939
questions.explanation: All three accept the basic facts of 1930-33; they disagree about the relative weight of structural, economic and short-term political causes. Evaluating such interpretations means weighing the evidence each uses.

questions.stem: In 1932 the Communist Party (KPD) attacked the Social Democrats (SPD) as 'social fascists'. Historians see this as important to Weimar's collapse because it:
options: convinced Hindenburg to appoint a Communist as Chancellor
divided the left and prevented a united front against the Nazis
persuaded the SPD to form a coalition with the Nazi Party
led the KPD to win a Reichstag majority and abolish the constitution
questions.explanation: Following Moscow's line, the KPD treated the SPD as its main enemy, so the two largest working-class parties never cooperated against Hitler. Together they still won more votes than the Nazis in November 1932.

questions.stem: A historian uses a 1932 Nazi election poster promising 'work and bread' to explain the party's rising vote. What is the main limitation of the poster as evidence for why Germans voted Nazi?
options: It was produced after 1945 and so reflects knowledge of the war
It was made by the Nazis' political opponents to make the party look foolish
It shows only the views of the SPD's working-class supporters
It shows what the party promised, not why individual voters chose it
questions.explanation: A poster is good evidence of the party's message and its targeting of the unemployed, but motives must be tested with other sources such as voting patterns, diaries and police reports. It was made by the Nazis in 1932, not later or by opponents.

questions.stem: Which German statesman, Chancellor in 1923 and Foreign Minister until 1929, ended passive resistance and negotiated the Locarno Treaties?
options: Gustav Stresemann
Heinrich Brüning
Franz von Papen
Friedrich Ebert
questions.explanation: Stresemann ended passive resistance in the Ruhr, oversaw the new currency, and as Foreign Minister won the Locarno Treaties and League membership. He died in October 1929, just before the Wall Street Crash.
